title: Green Sahara: why the desert dried
body:
Read the following extract, adapted from the practice passage 'Green Sahara' in the chapter.

Just 6,000 years ago, the Sahara was green. Prehistoric rock art shows hippopotamuses, which need year-round water. The green Sahara was the product of the migration of the paleo-monsoon. The tilt of the earth's axis varies in a regular cycle, the axis wobbles like a spinning top, and the date of the earth's perihelion, its closest approach to the sun, varies in a cycle as well. When the Northern Hemisphere tilted sharply towards the sun at the closest approach, the African monsoon shifted north, as it did 10,000 years ago, inundating North Africa. Around 5,000 years ago the monsoon shifted dramatically southward again. As the land dried out and vegetation decreased, the soil lost its ability to hold water. Fewer clouds formed from evaporation, and rain washed away and evaporated quickly. There was a kind of runaway drying effect. By 4,000 years ago the Sahara had become what it is today.
